filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Alpha Wrapping
filters.shortDescription: Generate a watertight alpha wrapping of the current mesh or point cloud using CGAL.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Compute an alpha wrapping with an offset around the current mesh and add the result as a new mesh layer. Alpha wrapping is useful for producing robust watertight approximations of defective, self-intersecting, open, or highly detailed input geometry. Smaller `Alpha` values follow the input more tightly but increase output complexity and computation time. `Offset` controls the clearance added around the input surface and must be strictly positive.

Faces are optional, but they are **used**, not merely a container for the vertices:

- A layer **with faces** is wrapped as a *triangle soup*. Triangle interiors are part of the input, so a large flat face is solid to the rolling ball, and CGAL subdivides oversized faces so that the spatial structure resolves at the `Alpha` scale.
- A layer with **only vertices** is wrapped as a *point set*, which makes this a point-cloud reconstruction method. Unlike Poisson-family reconstruction it needs no vertex normals, because the positive offset is what defines the envelope.

The two paths therefore give **different results on the same geometry**. Where a triangle spans a wide gap, the point-set path sees only its three corners and the ball can roll into the space between them, denting or holing the wrap. Wrap a point cloud only when the sampling is dense relative to `Alpha` and `Offset`; if the layer has faces, keep them.

The result is an *approximating* reconstruction: the offset is strictly positive, so the output surface never passes through the input points.

The filter uses CGAL's 3D Alpha Wrapping implementation.

Reference:
Cédric Portaneri, Mael Rouxel-Labbé, Michael Hemmer, David Cohen-Steiner, Pierre Alliez, **Alpha Wrapping with an Offset**, 2022.

Original MeshLab plugin contribution: Lex van der Sluijs, PTC.

parameters.label: Alpha
parameters.help: Radius of the rolling ball used by CGAL alpha wrapping. Smaller values produce a tighter and more detailed wrap, but increase computation time and output mesh size. MeshLab default: 2% of the bounding-box diagonal.

parameters.label: Offset
parameters.help: Positive offset added around the input surface. Larger values make a looser, more conservative envelope; very small values can make the computation heavier. MeshLab default: 0.1% of the bounding-box diagonal.

filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Alpha Shape
filters.shortDescription: Build the alpha complex or alpha shape of the current mesh or point cloud.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Builds the **alpha shape** of the current layer's vertices: the subcomplex of their Delaunay triangulation kept by a ball of radius `Alpha` that can reach it without enclosing any point. Small `Alpha` values give a sparse, pitted result; as `Alpha` grows the shape fills in and converges to the convex hull.

Only vertex positions are used, so a raw point cloud with no faces and no normals works — it is an *interpolating* reconstruction, meaning every output vertex is one of the input points.

**Output** selects what is written:

- *Alpha Shape* — the boundary of the alpha complex (CGAL `REGULAR` facets). This is the surface.
- *Alpha Complex* — also keeps the `SINGULAR` facets, the lower-dimensional sheets that the boundary drops. Useful for seeing what the complex contains, not for a clean surface.

Each face carries its **circumradius in face scalar**, so the scalar histogram shows the alpha distribution and helps pick a better value.

Facet orientation comes from the Delaunay triangulation and is not made globally coherent; run *Orient Faces Consistently* if you need it.

Implemented with CGAL's 3D Alpha Shapes.

Reference:
Herbert Edelsbrunner, Ernst P. Mucke, **Three-Dimensional Alpha Shapes**, ACM Transactions on Graphics 13(1), 1994.

parameters.label: Alpha
parameters.help: Radius of the probing ball, as a percentage of the bounding box diagonal. Small values carve the shape away; large values converge to the convex hull.

parameters.label: Output
parameters.help: Alpha Shape writes the boundary surface. Alpha Complex additionally writes the singular facets held by the complex.

filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Voronoi Filtering
filters.shortDescription: Reconstruct a surface from an unoriented point cloud with the Amenta-Bern crust.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Reconstructs a surface from the current layer's vertices using **Voronoi filtering**, the crust algorithm of Amenta and Bern. It needs **no vertex normals**, which is what distinguishes it from the Poisson-family filters.

How it works, in two Delaunay passes:

1. Triangulate the samples. For each sample the two *poles* are found — the Voronoi vertices of its cell farthest from it, one on each side. Poles approximate the medial axis, so they lie far from the surface.
2. Triangulate samples and poles together. A Delaunay triangle whose three corners are all samples cannot span the medial axis, so those triangles are the reconstructed surface.

This is an *interpolating* reconstruction: every output vertex is one of the input points, and no new positions are invented.

**Limitations**, inherent to the algorithm rather than this implementation: it assumes a **closed, well-sampled, noise-free** surface. Points lying on the convex hull have unbounded Voronoi cells and therefore no finite outer pole, so open boundaries stay ragged; noisy input scatters the poles and thins the crust. For scanned or noisy data prefer *Reconstruct Surface by Screened Poisson*.

**Threshold** discards Voronoi vertices farther from their sample than that multiple of the bounding box diagonal, keeping near-degenerate cells from throwing a pole off to infinity.

Built on CGAL's 3D Delaunay triangulation.

Reference:
Nina Amenta, Marshall Bern, **Surface Reconstruction by Voronoi Filtering**, Discrete & Computational Geometry 22(4), 1999.

parameters.label: Threshold
parameters.help: Discard Voronoi vertices farther from their sample than this multiple of the bounding box diagonal. Guards against near-degenerate cells sending a pole to infinity.

filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Scale Space
filters.shortDescription: Reconstruct a surface by smoothing the point set to a coarser scale, then meshing it.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Smooths the current layer's points for a number of iterations — moving them to a coarser *scale* at which a surface is easier to extract — and then triangulates the smoothed points.

Only vertex positions are used, so a raw point cloud with no faces and no normals works.

**Iterations** controls how far the point set is smoothed: more iterations tolerate more noise but lose detail. **Neighbors** and **Samples** configure the weighted-PCA smoother.

**Mesher** selects how the smoothed points are triangulated:

- *Alpha Shape* — uses **Alpha** as the probing radius, and can be asked to separate shells or to force a manifold result.
- *Advancing Front* — grows a triangulation outward and needs no radius.

Unlike the other interpolating reconstructions here, the output vertices are the **smoothed** positions, not the original points: this filter moves the geometry before meshing it. Keep the input layer if you need the originals.

Implemented with CGAL's 3D Scale-Space Surface Reconstruction.

Reference:
Thijs van Lankveld, Marc van Kreveld, Remco Veltkamp, **Watertight Scenes from Urban LiDAR and Planar Surfaces**, Computer Graphics Forum 32(5), 2013.

parameters.label: Smoothing Iterations
parameters.help: How many times the point set is smoothed before meshing. Zero meshes the points as they are; more iterations tolerate more noise but lose detail.

parameters.label: Mesher
parameters.help: How the smoothed points are triangulated. Alpha Shape uses the Alpha radius below; Advancing Front needs no radius.

parameters.label: Alpha
parameters.help: Probing ball radius for the Alpha Shape mesher, as a percentage of the bounding box diagonal. Ignored by the Advancing Front mesher.

parameters.label: Neighbors
parameters.help: Number of nearest neighbours used by the weighted-PCA smoother at each point.

parameters.label: Samples
parameters.help: Number of points sampled to estimate the smoothing neighbourhood radius.

parameters.label: Force Manifold
parameters.help: Ask the Alpha Shape mesher for a manifold result, dropping the facets that would violate it.

parameters.label: Separate Shells
parameters.help: Keep separate shells of the Alpha Shape mesher's output apart instead of merging them.

filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Advancing Front
filters.shortDescription: Reconstruct a surface from an unoriented point cloud by growing a triangulation outward.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Grows a triangulation outward from a seed facet, repeatedly choosing the most plausible candidate triangle on the advancing boundary. It is an **interpolating** reconstruction: every output vertex is one of the input points, and no normals are required.

**Radius Ratio Bound** rejects candidate triangles whose circumradius is more than this multiple of the shortest edge, which is what stops the front from bridging across gaps. Raise it on sparse or uneven sampling; lower it to keep holes open rather than filling them with sliver triangles.

**Beta** is half the angle of the wedge in which only the triangle radius decides plausibility.

This is CGAL's counterpart to the *Reconstruct Surface by Ball Pivoting* filters: both grow a surface outward and interpolate the input points, but they are different algorithms and are worth comparing on the same cloud. CGAL has no ball-pivoting implementation of its own.

Implemented with CGAL's Advancing Front Surface Reconstruction.

Reference:
David Cohen-Steiner, Frank Da, **A greedy Delaunay-based surface reconstruction algorithm**, The Visual Computer 20(1), 2004.

parameters.label: Radius Ratio Bound
parameters.help: Reject a candidate triangle whose circumradius exceeds this multiple of its shortest edge. Larger values close more holes; smaller values leave sparse regions open.

parameters.label: Beta (degrees)
parameters.help: Half the angle of the wedge in which only the triangle radius counts towards plausibility. CGAL's default is 0.52 rad, about 30 degrees.

filters.name: Orient Point Cloud Normals
filters.shortDescription: Make an unoriented normal field consistently point outward, using a minimum spanning tree.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Orients the vertex normals of a point cloud so that neighbouring normals agree in sign, by propagating orientation along a **minimum spanning tree of the Riemannian graph** (Hoppe et al.).

This is the missing step between normal *estimation* and surface *reconstruction*. Filters such as *Compute Point Cloud Normals* fit a local surface and give each normal an arbitrary sign; Poisson-family and kinetic reconstruction all need normals that consistently point outward, and produce unusable results otherwise.

**Neighbors** sets how many nearest neighbours are linked in the Riemannian graph. Larger values bridge gaps in sparse data but can propagate orientation across thin structures that should stay separate.

A cloud in several disconnected pieces cannot be oriented as a whole: the normals of every component after the first are reported as unoriented and left untouched. Enable **Remove Unoriented Vertices** to delete them instead.

Implemented with CGAL's Point Set Processing.

Reference:
Hugues Hoppe, Tony DeRose, Tom Duchamp, John McDonald, Werner Stuetzle, **Surface Reconstruction from Unorganized Points**, SIGGRAPH 1992.

parameters.label: Neighbors
parameters.help: Number of nearest neighbours linked in the Riemannian graph. Larger values bridge sparse regions but risk propagating orientation across thin structures.

parameters.label: Remove Unoriented Vertices
parameters.help: Delete the vertices whose normals could not be oriented instead of leaving them untouched. They are usually disconnected components.

filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Poisson (CGAL)
filters.shortDescription: Reconstruct a watertight surface from oriented points with CGAL's Poisson solver.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Solves the Poisson equation for an implicit function whose gradient best matches the input normal field, then extracts its zero level set.

It differs from *Reconstruct Surface by Screened Poisson* in how that level set is **meshed**: CGAL uses Delaunay refinement rather than marching cubes, so the output is manifold with well-shaped triangles and a size driven by the sampling, at the cost of being slower. The two are worth comparing on the same cloud — that is why both are here.

**Requires oriented normals.** If the layer has none, run *Compute Point Cloud Normals* and then *Orient Point Cloud Normals* first.

Triangle size and quality are controlled relative to the estimated average point spacing:

- **Minimum Angle** — the lower bound on triangle angles, in degrees.
- **Maximum Radius** — largest triangle circumradius, as a multiple of the spacing.
- **Approximation Error** — how far the mesh may deviate from the level set, as a multiple of the spacing.

Implemented with CGAL's Poisson Surface Reconstruction.

Reference:
Michael Kazhdan, Matthew Bolitho, Hugues Hoppe, **Poisson Surface Reconstruction**, Symposium on Geometry Processing 2006.

parameters.label: Minimum Angle (degrees)
parameters.help: Lower bound on the angles of the output triangles. Lower values are easier to satisfy; CGAL's default is 20.

parameters.label: Maximum Radius
parameters.help: Largest triangle circumradius, as a multiple of the estimated average point spacing. Smaller values give a denser mesh.

parameters.label: Approximation Error
parameters.help: How far the mesh may deviate from the implicit surface, as a multiple of the average point spacing. Smaller values follow the data more closely and cost more.

parameters.label: Perturb the input
parameters.help: Displace every input point by about a millionth of the bounding-box diagonal before reconstructing. Far below any modelling tolerance, and invisible in the result, but it breaks the exact symmetries that can stop CGAL's surface mesher terminating -- an analytically generated sphere or cylinder, where every point lies exactly on the same surface, is the case that needs it. Leave it off for scanned or otherwise noisy data, which is never degenerate in this way. The displacement is deterministic, so a run stays reproducible.

parameters.label: Spacing Neighbors
parameters.help: Number of neighbours used to estimate the average point spacing that the three settings above are relative to.

filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Kinetic Partition
filters.shortDescription: Reconstruct a piecewise-planar surface from oriented points by kinetic space partition and min-cut.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
A piecewise-planar reconstruction pipeline, run end to end by this one filter:

1. **Shape detection** finds planar regions in the point cloud.
2. **Regularization** aligns those planes where they are nearly parallel, coplanar or orthogonal.
3. **Kinetic space partition** propagates the planes until they collide, cutting the bounding box into convex volumes.
4. **Min-cut** labels each volume inside or outside; the surface is the boundary between the two labels.

Because the output is built from detected planes rather than fitted to the samples, it is planar **by construction** — which suits buildings, rooms and other man-made shapes far better than a smooth reconstruction, and is quite unsuitable for organic ones.

**Requires oriented normals.** Run *Compute Point Cloud Normals* and then *Orient Point Cloud Normals* first if the layer has none.

**Maximum Distance** is the most important setting: it is how far a point may sit from a plane and still belong to it, so it must be set to the scale of the noise in the data. **Lambda** trades faithfulness against simplicity — higher values give fewer, larger facets.

The reconstruction emits convex polygons, which this filter fan-triangulates because MeshLab stores triangle meshes.

Implemented with CGAL's Kinetic Surface Reconstruction.

Reference:
Sven Oesau, Florent Lafarge, **Kinetic Shape Reconstruction**, ACM Transactions on Graphics 39(5), 2020.

parameters.label: Maximum Distance
parameters.help: How far a point may lie from a plane and still be assigned to it. Set this to the noise scale of the data; it is the setting that most affects the result.

parameters.label: Maximum Angle (degrees)
parameters.help: Largest angle between a point's normal and its plane's normal for the point to be assigned to that plane.

parameters.label: Lambda
parameters.help: Trades data faithfulness against model complexity, in [0, 1). Higher values give a simpler surface with fewer facets.

parameters.label: Minimum Region Size
parameters.help: Smallest number of points a detected planar region must contain to be kept.

parameters.label: Neighbors
parameters.help: Number of nearest neighbours used when growing planar regions.

parameters.label: Intersections
parameters.help: How many times propagating planes may intersect before the partition stops. Higher values give a finer partition and cost considerably more.

filters.name: Create Mesh Bounding Box
filters.shortDescription: Turn the current layer's bounding box into a mesh of its own.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Creates a new layer holding the bounding box of the current layer as an actual eight-vertex, twelve-triangle box, rather than as an annotation drawn over the viewport. Useful whenever the box has to be *operated on* — measured, exported, intersected, used as a crop volume or as a stand-in for the object in a larger scene.

**Alignment** chooses between the three boxes worth having:

- **Axis aligned** is the box the viewport draws: the smallest box whose sides are parallel to the layer's own axes. It is exact, instant, and depends on how the object happens to be oriented.
- **Oriented** is the smallest box in *any* orientation, found by searching the space of rotations. For an object lying at an angle it is dramatically tighter than the axis-aligned one; for an object already aligned to its axes the two coincide. The search is an approximation, not a proven optimum, and it costs time on large inputs — it runs on the convex hull, so cost follows the hull rather than the vertex count.
- **Oriented, turning the layer** finds the same box and then turns the object instead of the box: the rotation is written into the layer's transformation, so the layer comes to rest on the axes and the box is created axis-aligned alongside it. The vertices are not touched — only the matrix — which is how you straighten an object that was digitised or exported at an arbitrary angle.

The new layer inherits the source layer's matrix, so the box sits on the object wherever the object has been moved to.

To box the whole scene rather than one layer, use **Create Scene Bounding Box**.

The oriented box is computed with CGAL's Optimal Bounding Box package.

Reference:
Konstantinos Katrioplas, Mael Rouxel-Labbé, **Optimal Bounding Box**, CGAL User and Reference Manual, CGAL Editorial Board.

parameters.label: Alignment
parameters.help: Axis aligned is the box the viewport draws, parallel to the layer's own axes. Oriented searches for the smallest box in any orientation, which is much tighter for an object lying at an angle but costs time to find.

filters.name: Create Scene Bounding Box
filters.shortDescription: Turn the bounding box of every visible layer into a mesh of its own.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Creates a new layer holding the bounding box of the **whole scene**: one box around every *visible* layer, measured in world space so each layer's own transformation is taken into account. Hidden layers are ignored, which is how you box a subset — hide what should not count and run it again.

The box is created in world space with an identity transformation, so it stays put whatever the layers it was measured from do afterwards.

**Alignment** chooses between the two boxes worth having:

- **Axis aligned** is the smallest box whose sides are parallel to the world axes — the extent the viewport frames to.
- **Oriented** is the smallest box in *any* orientation. For a scene laid out at an angle it is much tighter; for one already square to the axes the two coincide. The search is an approximation, not a proven optimum, and it costs time on large scenes — it runs on the convex hull, so cost follows the hull rather than the total vertex count.

There is deliberately no *turning the scene* option: straightening is a per-layer operation, and **Create Mesh Bounding Box** offers it for the current layer.

The oriented box is computed with CGAL's Optimal Bounding Box package.

Reference:
Konstantinos Katrioplas, Mael Rouxel-Labbé, **Optimal Bounding Box**, CGAL User and Reference Manual, CGAL Editorial Board.

parameters.label: Alignment
parameters.help: Axis aligned is the smallest box parallel to the world axes. Oriented searches for the smallest box in any orientation, which is much tighter for a scene laid out at an angle but costs time to find.
